Appendix A Additional Methods Details

This appendix collects the reproducibility details deferred from Section 2. Notation, symbols, and labels follow the main text.

A.1 Data construction details

Full experimental condition and drug-level collapsing.

Each Tahoe-100M pseudobulk_differential_expression record is indexed by a full experimental condition

d~=(d,dose,plate),\tilde{d}=(d,\mathrm{dose},\mathrm{plate}), (14)

where dd is the drug identity, and provides DESeq2-style statistics

(baseMean,log2FoldChange,lfcSE,stat,pvalue,padj),(\texttt{baseMean},\texttt{log2FoldChange},\texttt{lfcSE},\texttt{stat},\texttt{pvalue},\texttt{padj}), (15)

together with drug, concentration, plate, and cell-line identifiers and the number of treated and control cells. At the condition granularity we write Δc,d~,g:=log2FoldChange\Delta_{c,\tilde{d},g}:=\texttt{log2FoldChange}, qc,d~,g:=padjq_{c,\tilde{d},g}:=\texttt{padj}, and μc,d~,g:=baseMean\mu_{c,\tilde{d},g}:=\texttt{baseMean}. Records with missing Δ\Delta or qq are discarded, and to avoid unstable labels from underpowered comparisons we retain only conditions with treated-group cell count nc,d~trt≥30n^{\mathrm{trt}}_{c,\tilde{d}}\geq 30.

The gene-centered task of Section 2.1 requires one record per (c,d,g)(c,d,g) for primary label assignment and confidence weighting. For these two purposes, we merge the surviving conditions d~\tilde{d} that share the drug identity dd by keeping the record with the largest |Δc,d~,g||\Delta_{c,\tilde{d},g}|, and write Δc,d,g\Delta_{c,d,g}, qc,d,gq_{c,d,g}, μc,d,g\mu_{c,d,g} for the statistics of the retained record. A separate reward-side condition table retains d~\tilde{d}, so pathway-response proxies are computed within individual conditions rather than from these collapsed gene-level records. The collapsing rule makes the primary drug-level label semantics deliberately asymmetric: a directional label asserts that at least one tested condition surviving quality control reached the thresholds of Section 2.2, whereas a No\mathrm{No} label asserts the complementary statement that no such condition provided directional evidence. Selecting the strongest available effect shifts the drug-level label distribution toward directional calls and raises the typical retained |Δ||\Delta| relative to a dose-averaged summary; it should therefore be interpreted as a maximum-observed-response endpoint rather than a dose-invariant effect.

Confidence weighting.

Each triplet with yg∈𝒴y_{g}\in\mathcal{Y} carries a confidence weight wc,d,gconf∈[0.1,1]w^{\mathrm{conf}}_{c,d,g}\in[0.1,1] computed from (Δ,q,μ)=(Δc,d,g,qc,d,g,μc,d,g)(\Delta,q,\mu)=(\Delta_{c,d,g},q_{c,d,g},\mu_{c,d,g}). For Up\mathrm{Up} or Down\mathrm{Down},

wconfc,d,g=max[0.1,\displaystyle w^{\mathrm{conf}}_{c,d,g}=\max\Big[0.1, clip⁡(|Δ|2, 0, 1)\displaystyle\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\tfrac{|\Delta|}{2},\,0,\,1\right) (16)
⋅clip(−log10⁡(max⁡(q, 10−300))5, 0, 1)],\displaystyle\cdot\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\tfrac{-\log_{10}(\max(q,\,10^{-300}))}{5},\,0,\,1\right)\Big],

and for No\mathrm{No},

wconfc,d,g=max[0.1,\displaystyle w^{\mathrm{conf}}_{c,d,g}=\max\Big[0.1, clip⁡(log10⁡(μ+1)log10⁡(101), 0, 1)\displaystyle\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\tfrac{\log_{10}(\mu+1)}{\log_{10}(101)},\,0,\,1\right) (17)
⋅clip(0.20−|Δ|0.20, 0, 1)].\displaystyle\cdot\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\tfrac{0.20-|\Delta|}{0.20},\,0,\,1\right)\Big].

These weights give larger effective supervision to strong, significant directional calls and to high-expression, near-zero-effect null calls, while every triplet retains its assigned label. Where the weight enters the RL update is specified in Section 2.4 and formalized in Appendix A.4.

Split, class stratification, and leakage.

Before quality control or triplet construction, every Tahoe-100M sample is assigned by cell line. All samples from the five lines listed in Section 2.2 form the held-out test domain, and all samples from every other cell line form the development domain. After applying the same eligibility and label rules within both domains, development (c,d,g)(c,d,g) groups are split 90:10 into training and validation partitions, stratified by cell line and label; records sharing a (c,d,g)(c,d,g) key cannot cross this boundary. Because the outer partition is over cell lines rather than drugs or genes, a drug or gene may occur in both development and test domains in different cell contexts. A supporting case may share the current query’s (d,g)(d,g) pair only when it comes from the training partition and is then treated as cross-context evidence. The current query, its repeated measurements, validation outcomes, and all held-out-cell outcomes are excluded from retrieval. Single-cell replicates are already aggregated in the Tahoe-100M pseudobulk statistics, so each candidate example corresponds to one eligible cell-line–perturbation–gene record. We retain every eligible triplet and use cell-line-, drug-, and label-stratified batches and prompt streams to control optimization imbalance; no class, cell line, or drug is capped or downsampled. The leakage controls in Section 2.2 apply throughout: no query-specific expression measurement enters the model side, and pathway supervision is available only on the reward side.

A.2 Trajectory and SFT details

Retrieval configuration.

The retrieval module aligns entities from PubChem, DrugBank, UniProt, Gene Ontology, Reactome, STRING, and CORUM by standard identifiers, filters high-frequency low-information nodes and duplicate facts before prompt construction, and computes drug and gene similarity from semantic annotation and knowledge-graph topology, restricted to 𝒞train\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{train}}. Cell-context similarity is computed only from outcome-independent tissue, lineage, and curated genotype annotations; no perturbation-response-derived expression feature is used for retrieval or ranking. Contrastive cases are retrieved separately from each outcome group and united as 𝒮⁡(x)=𝒮Up​(x)∪𝒮Down​(x)∪𝒮No​(x)\mathcal{S}(x)=\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Up}}(x)\cup\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Down}}(x)\cup\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{No}}(x). A training case from another cell line may share the query’s (d,g)(d,g) pair and is then included only as cross-context evidence; the current query, its repeated measurements, and every held-out-cell outcome are excluded. The assembled context is

𝒦⁡(x)=(knowledge-graph evidence for ​(c,d,g),𝒮⁡(x)).\mathcal{K}(x)=\big(\text{knowledge-graph evidence for }(c,d,g),\ \mathcal{S}(x)\big). (18)

No expression measurement or label of the current query enters 𝒦⁡(x)\mathcal{K}(x), so inference relies solely on knowledge-graph evidence and outcome-stratified training cases with their historical outcomes. Figure 7 summarizes the resulting model-visible prompt fields, required response order, and reward-side quantities that are withheld from the prompt.

Model-generated trajectory sampling.

Given 𝒦⁡(x)\mathcal{K}(x), the current Qwen3-4B policy generates MM candidate trajectories,

z~m,y^m∼πθ0(⋅∣x,𝒦(x)),m=1,…,M,\tilde{z}_{m},\hat{y}_{m}\sim\pi_{\theta_{0}}(\cdot\mid x,\mathcal{K}(x)),\qquad m=1,\dots,M, (19)

where θ0\theta_{0} denotes the Qwen3-4B Base parameters before any PertMind-specific update, rather than an external teacher, and M=8M=8. The model is prompted to (1) identify the perturbation’s direct targets and mechanism of action, (2) compare retrieved cases to the current drug, gene, and cell context, (3) predict a direction for every supplied candidate pathway, (4) propagate pathway-level change to the regulation of the target gene, and (5) output a single Up\mathrm{Up}, Down\mathrm{Down}, or No\mathrm{No} conclusion. Trusted-trajectory checks are implemented as reproducible validators: deterministic parsers verify the unique terminal label, required pathway slots, and output order; every factual entity–relation claim must cite an identifier present in the prompt-visible evidence, while uncited statements must be marked explicitly as inference; and required structured fields verify the presence of a perturbation-target–pathway–gene chain. Together with final-label correctness, these checks instantiate the five criteria of Section 2.3. Retained trajectories form 𝒟traj={(x,z⋆,yg)}\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{traj}}=\{(x,z^{\star},y_{g})\}.

Balanced Fine-Tuning objective.

For sample bb with reference response tokens yb⋆y^{\star}_{b}, let

cb,t=πθ​(yb,t⋆∣yb,<t⋆,xb),ℓb,t=−log⁡cb,t.c_{b,t}=\pi_{\theta}(y^{\star}_{b,t}\mid y^{\star}_{b,<t},x_{b}),\qquad\ell_{b,t}=-\log c_{b,t}. (20)

Using a local window of gBFT=256g_{\mathrm{BFT}}=256 response tokens around tt, let Wb,tW_{b,t} denote the valid response-token indices in that window after clipping it at sequence boundaries, and define the local context confidence

Cb,tloc=1|Wb,t|​∑j∈Wb,tcb,j,C^{\mathrm{loc}}_{b,t}=\frac{1}{|W_{b,t}|}\sum_{j\in W_{b,t}}c_{b,j}, (21)

the locally normalized token weight

ρb,t=clip⁡(cb,tCb,tloc+ϵ, 0, 1),wb,tBFT=sg⁡(ρb,t),\rho_{b,t}=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\frac{c_{b,t}}{C^{\mathrm{loc}}_{b,t}+\epsilon},\,0,\,1\right),\qquad w^{\mathrm{BFT}}_{b,t}=\operatorname{sg}(\rho_{b,t}), (22)

and the sequence-level difficulty weight

pbconf=mint⁡Cb,tloc,sb=sg⁡(1−pbconf),p^{\mathrm{conf}}_{b}=\min_{t}C^{\mathrm{loc}}_{b,t},\qquad s_{b}=\operatorname{sg}(1-p^{\mathrm{conf}}_{b}), (23)

where sg\operatorname{sg} denotes stop-gradient. The BFT objective, used as the SFT loss on 𝒟traj\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{traj}}, is

ℒSFT​(θ)=1B​∑b=1Bsb​∑tmb,t​wb,tBFT​ℓb,t∑tmb,t+ϵ,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}s_{b}\frac{\sum_{t}m_{b,t}w^{\mathrm{BFT}}_{b,t}\ell_{b,t}}{\sum_{t}m_{b,t}+\epsilon}, (24)

where mb,tm_{b,t} masks non-response tokens and ϵ>0\epsilon>0 is a numerical stabilizer. Isolated low-confidence tokens embedded in high-confidence contexts are down-weighted; because sbs_{b} depends on the minimum local confidence, trajectories containing at least one difficult local span receive larger relative sequence-level weights than easier trajectories. All confidence-derived quantities carry a stop-gradient so that the model cannot lower the loss by manipulating weights instead of raising the likelihood of y⋆y^{\star}. One epoch on 𝒟traj\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{traj}} produces the SFT policy πθSFT\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{SFT}}}, which is retained as both the GRPO initialization and the fixed KL reference in Appendix A.4.

A.3 Pathway supervision details

Candidate pathway selection.

We collect Reactome pathways containing the target gene,

𝒫0​(g)={P:g∈P},\mathcal{P}_{0}(g)=\{P:g\in P\}, (25)

and retain by default only pathways with 10≤|P|≤20010\leq|P|\leq 200 members. For each candidate the non-target member set is P−g=P∖{g}P^{-g}=P\setminus\{g\}; the target gene is excluded from every subsequent pathway score so that its own expression cannot leak into the auxiliary reward. Candidates are ranked using only information that is available before any (c,d)(c,d)-specific expression outcome is examined,

Rcand​(P∣d,g)=αgene​Rgenecand​(P∣g)+αdrug​Rdrugcand​(P∣d),R_{\mathrm{cand}}(P\mid d,g)=\alpha_{\mathrm{gene}}R^{\mathrm{cand}}_{\mathrm{gene}}(P\mid g)+\alpha_{\mathrm{drug}}R^{\mathrm{cand}}_{\mathrm{drug}}(P\mid d), (26)

where Rgenecand​(P∣g)R^{\mathrm{cand}}_{\mathrm{gene}}(P\mid g) scores the curated strength or confidence of target-gene membership in the pathway and Rdrugcand​(P∣d)R^{\mathrm{cand}}_{\mathrm{drug}}(P\mid d) quantifies drug–pathway relevance. We use αgene=0.60\alpha_{\mathrm{gene}}=0.60 and αdrug=0.40\alpha_{\mathrm{drug}}=0.40. Drug relevance is prioritized in the following order: a direct drug target within the pathway; a target within one or two hops of pathway members in a high-confidence interaction network; or shared membership on a manually curated mechanism-of-action axis. When no reliable drug-mechanism annotation is available, this term is recorded as unknown rather than inferred speculatively. The top-ranked candidates are kept, at most 3 per query, as 𝒫cand​(d,g)\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{cand}}(d,g). Both the filter and the ranking are computed before the (c,d)(c,d)-specific differential-expression outcome is examined and depend only on curated target/pathway membership and drug-target or drug–pathway knowledge, so candidate selection is reproducible at inference time and outcome-independent.

Condition-level pathway-response proxy.

Label construction may use training-split expression statistics, but the resulting label is used only for reward computation, never as model input. Pathway scores are always computed inside a single complete experimental condition so that every member entering a score shares the same dose and plate. Let 𝒯⁡(c,d)\mathcal{T}(c,d) denote the set of quality-controlled conditions d~=(d,dose,plate)\tilde{d}=(d,\mathrm{dose},\mathrm{plate}) for drug dd in cell line cc that survive the filters of Appendix A.1. For each P∈𝒫cand​(d,g)P\in\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{cand}}(d,g) and each d~∈𝒯⁡(c,d)\tilde{d}\in\mathcal{T}(c,d), let H⁡(P,c,d~,g)⊆P−gH(P,c,\tilde{d},g)\subseteq P^{-g} denote the non-target members with finite Δc,d~,h\Delta_{c,\tilde{d},h} and qc,d~,hq_{c,\tilde{d},h} under a condition satisfying nc,d~trt≥30n^{\mathrm{trt}}_{c,\tilde{d}}\geq 30. The entire set is drawn from a single (c,d~)(c,\tilde{d}), so HH never mixes members measured at different doses or on different plates. For h∈H⁡(P,c,d~,g)h\in H(P,c,\tilde{d},g), define the condition-level significance-weighted signed effect

uh,d~=Δc,d~,h⋅clip⁡(−log10⁡(max⁡(qc,d~,h,qmin)),0,amax),u_{h,\tilde{d}}=\Delta_{c,\tilde{d},h}\cdot\operatorname{clip}\!\left(-\log_{10}(\max(q_{c,\tilde{d},h},q_{\min})),0,a_{\max}\right), (27)

where qmin=10−6q_{\min}=10^{-6} is a fixed lower bound and amax=6a_{\max}=6 caps the influence of any single, extremely small qq-value. The condition-level pathway aggregate score is

SP,d~=∑h∈H⁡(P,c,d~,g)wh​uh,d~∑h∈H⁡(P,c,d~,g)wh,S_{P,\tilde{d}}=\frac{\sum_{h\in H(P,c,\tilde{d},g)}w_{h}\,u_{h,\tilde{d}}}{\sum_{h\in H(P,c,\tilde{d},g)}w_{h}}, (28)

with wh=1w_{h}=1 by default; non-uniform, outcome-independent topological weights are used only when pre-registered. The condition-level fraction of nonzero-effect members whose sign agrees with the aggregate direction is

CP,d~=|{h∈H(P,c,d~,g):sign(uh,d~)=sign(SP,d~),uh,d~≠0}||{h∈H⁡(P,c,d~,g):uh,d~≠0}|,C_{P,\tilde{d}}=\frac{|\{h\in H(P,c,\tilde{d},g):\operatorname{sign}(u_{h,\tilde{d}})=\operatorname{sign}(S_{P,\tilde{d}}),\ u_{h,\tilde{d}}\neq 0\}|}{|\{h\in H(P,c,\tilde{d},g):u_{h,\tilde{d}}\neq 0\}|}, (29)

with the convention CP,d~=0C_{P,\tilde{d}}=0 when no member has nonzero effect. The condition-level fraction of significantly responding members is

AP,d~=|{h∈H⁡(P,c,d~,g):qc,d~,h≤0.05∧|Δc,d~,h|≥0.585}||H⁡(P,c,d~,g)|.A_{P,\tilde{d}}=\frac{|\{h\in H(P,c,\tilde{d},g):q_{c,\tilde{d},h}\leq 0.05\ \land\ |\Delta_{c,\tilde{d},h}|\geq 0.585\}|}{|H(P,c,\tilde{d},g)|}. (30)

The condition-level pathway-response proxy label is

yP,d~={uncertain,|H⁡(P,c,d~,g)|<5,Up,SP,d~≥τdir∧CP,d~≥γ,Down,SP,d~≤−τdir∧CP,d~≥γ,No,|SP,d~|≤τno∧AP,d~≤ηno,uncertain,otherwise,y_{P,\tilde{d}}=\begin{cases}\mathrm{uncertain},&|H(P,c,\tilde{d},g)|<5,\\ \mathrm{Up},&S_{P,\tilde{d}}\geq\tau_{\mathrm{dir}}\ \land\ C_{P,\tilde{d}}\geq\gamma,\\ \mathrm{Down},&S_{P,\tilde{d}}\leq-\tau_{\mathrm{dir}}\ \land\ C_{P,\tilde{d}}\geq\gamma,\\ \mathrm{No},&|S_{P,\tilde{d}}|\leq\tau_{\mathrm{no}}\ \land\ A_{P,\tilde{d}}\leq\eta_{\mathrm{no}},\\ \mathrm{uncertain},&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (31)

with γ=0.60\gamma=0.60, τdir=0.20\tau_{\mathrm{dir}}=0.20, τno=0.05\tau_{\mathrm{no}}=0.05, and ηno=0.20\eta_{\mathrm{no}}=0.20. The directional and null cutoffs are constrained to satisfy

0≤τno<τdir,0\leq\tau_{\mathrm{no}}<\tau_{\mathrm{dir}}, (32)

so the directional region |SP,d~|≥τdir|S_{P,\tilde{d}}|\geq\tau_{\mathrm{dir}} and the null region |SP,d~|≤τno|S_{P,\tilde{d}}|\leq\tau_{\mathrm{no}} are disjoint. All parameters are fixed on the development split before evaluation on the held-out cell lines. Requiring both a small aggregate effect and a low fraction of significantly responding members for No\mathrm{No} prevents mislabeling a pathway with large but mutually canceling up- and down-regulated members as unresponsive. Conditions with fewer than five reliable non-target members or with effects in the gray zone are labeled uncertain\mathrm{uncertain} at the condition level. We refer to yP,d~y_{P,\tilde{d}} as a transcriptional pathway-response proxy: it summarizes the coordinated transcriptional response of the pathway’s non-target members under a single (c,d~)(c,\tilde{d}) and is not a direct measurement of protein activity, metabolic flux, or causal pathway activation.

Cross-condition consensus for drug-level pathway labels.

The drug-level label yP​(c,d,g)y_{P}(c,d,g) used by the reward in Section 2.4 is obtained by a conservative consensus over the determinate condition-level labels in {yP,d~:d~∈𝒯⁡(c,d)}\{y_{P,\tilde{d}}:\tilde{d}\in\mathcal{T}(c,d)\}, so that no drug-level directional or null call is issued when determinate conditions disagree. Conditions labeled uncertain\mathrm{uncertain} are ignored by the consensus, and a single determinate condition can supply the drug-level label. Let

ℒP,c,d,g={yP,d~:d~∈𝒯(c,d),yP,d~≠uncertain}\mathcal{L}_{P,c,d,g}=\{y_{P,\tilde{d}}:\tilde{d}\in\mathcal{T}(c,d),\ y_{P,\tilde{d}}\neq\mathrm{uncertain}\} (33)

be the set of determinate condition-level labels. Then

yP​(c,d,g)={uncertain,ℒP,c,d,g=∅,Up,ℒP,c,d,g≠∅∧ℒP,c,d,g⊆{Up},Down,ℒP,c,d,g≠∅∧ℒP,c,d,g⊆{Down},No,ℒP,c,d,g≠∅∧ℒP,c,d,g⊆{No},uncertain,otherwise.y_{P}(c,d,g)=\begin{cases}\mathrm{uncertain},&\mathcal{L}_{P,c,d,g}=\emptyset,\\ \mathrm{Up},&\mathcal{L}_{P,c,d,g}\neq\emptyset\ \land\ \mathcal{L}_{P,c,d,g}\subseteq\{\mathrm{Up}\},\\ \mathrm{Down},&\mathcal{L}_{P,c,d,g}\neq\emptyset\ \land\ \mathcal{L}_{P,c,d,g}\subseteq\{\mathrm{Down}\},\\ \mathrm{No},&\mathcal{L}_{P,c,d,g}\neq\emptyset\ \land\ \mathcal{L}_{P,c,d,g}\subseteq\{\mathrm{No}\},\\ \mathrm{uncertain},&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (34)

A drug with a single determinate condition inherits that condition’s label; a drug with multiple determinate conditions receives a directional or null drug-level label only when all determinate condition-level labels agree, and any disagreement among those determinate labels is mapped to uncertain\mathrm{uncertain}. Because the consensus is taken over pre-computed condition-level labels, no drug-level pathway score ever fuses members measured at different doses or on different plates. uncertain\mathrm{uncertain} triplets remain in the main-task training pool and are simply excluded from the pathway reward term.

Model-visible information and pathway masking.

The prompt lists the complete retained candidate set 𝒫cand​(d,g)\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{cand}}(d,g); for each listed candidate it includes the pathway name, its documented relation to the drug and target gene, and a small number of representative non-target members selected once per pathway using the same pre-registered static score combining annotation confidence and outcome-independent network centrality. This fixed member selection never consults the current condition’s expression statistics. The prompt never includes the pathway’s proxy direction, the expression effect, pp-value, or qq-value of any member under any condition, the intermediate quantities SP,d~S_{P,\tilde{d}}, CP,d~C_{P,\tilde{d}}, or AP,d~A_{P,\tilde{d}}, or any reordering of candidates based on the realized outcome. In particular, the prompt does not indicate which candidates received a determinate yP​(c,d,g)y_{P}(c,d,g). The scored subset used in Section 2.4 is

𝒫det​(c,d,g)={P∈𝒫cand​(d,g):yP​(c,d,g)≠uncertain},K=|𝒫det​(c,d,g)|,\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{det}}(c,d,g)=\{P\in\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{cand}}(d,g):y_{P}(c,d,g)\neq\mathrm{uncertain}\},\qquad K=\big|\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{det}}(c,d,g)\big|, (35)

and the pathway mask

mpw=𝟏[K>0]∈{0,1}m_{\mathrm{pw}}=\mathbf{1}[K>0]\in\{0,1\} (36)

is redundant with the Rpw:=0R_{\mathrm{pw}}:=0 convention when K=0K=0; it is kept explicit because the training code applies it as a per-sample mask when reducing rewards over a batch. Triplets whose candidates all turn out uncertain\mathrm{uncertain} remain in the main-task training pool and are simply excluded from the pathway reward term, so pathway augmentation increases supervision density without restricting the training corpus.

A.4 Full optimization definition

Grouped rollouts.

GRPO trains on every triplet in 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} with a determinate primary label, not only the trusted-trajectory subset used for SFT. For each prompt xx, a group of G=8G=8 responses oio_{i}, i=1,…,Gi=1,\dots,G, is sampled from the current policy conditioned on the same biological context 𝒦⁡(x)\mathcal{K}(x). Each response contains structured pathway predictions, a mechanistic explanation, and a final gene-level label, and is scored by R⁡(oi)R(o_{i}) as in Section 2.4. The auxiliary weights are λpw=0.15\lambda_{\mathrm{pw}}=0.15 and λfmt=0.05\lambda_{\mathrm{fmt}}=0.05, selected on the held-out validation subset of the development domain and fixed before evaluation on 𝒞test\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{test}}.

Group standardization and confidence scaling.

The standardized advantage

A^i=R⁡(oi)−meanj⁡R⁡(oj)stdj⁡R⁡(oj)+ϵ\hat{A}_{i}=\frac{R(o_{i})-\operatorname{mean}_{j}R(o_{j})}{\operatorname{std}_{j}R(o_{j})+\epsilon} (37)

gives zero-variance groups a vanishing gradient contribution; such groups are uninformative rather than harmful. When the primary term alone is uniform across a group, it does not affect the within-group ranking, so the auxiliary terms provide the remaining preference signal. Confidence is applied after group standardization as a positive per-triplet multiplier on the complete sample objective, and never as an additional scaling of A^i\hat{A}_{i} itself, so that the within-group ranking induced by {A^i}i=1G\{\hat{A}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G} is unchanged and the shared positive constant wc,d,gconfw^{\mathrm{conf}}_{c,d,g} enters below at the objective level to uniformly scale the entire parameter update contributed by that triplet.

Clipped, KL-regularized policy optimization.

The behavior policy πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}} that generated the current rollouts is refreshed at every rollout iteration and is used only to define the clipped importance ratio below; it is distinct from the frozen SFT reference πθSFT\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{SFT}}}, which enters the objective only through the KL penalty. Let the token-level importance ratio against the behavior policy be

ri,t​(θ)=πθ​(oi,t∣x,𝒦⁡(x),oi,<t)πθold​(oi,t∣x,𝒦⁡(x),oi,<t),r_{i,t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{i,t}\mid x,\mathcal{K}(x),o_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(o_{i,t}\mid x,\mathcal{K}(x),o_{i,<t})}, (38)

and, separately, let

κi,t​(θ)=πθSFT​(oi,t∣x,𝒦⁡(x),oi,<t)πθ​(oi,t∣x,𝒦⁡(x),oi,<t)\kappa_{i,t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{SFT}}}(o_{i,t}\mid x,\mathcal{K}(x),o_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\theta}(o_{i,t}\mid x,\mathcal{K}(x),o_{i,<t})} (39)

denote a sampled-token ratio of the frozen SFT reference to the current policy, evaluated only at the sampled token oi,to_{i,t}. The symbol κi,t\kappa_{i,t} is deliberately distinct from the behavior ratio ri,tr_{i,t}: its denominator is πθ\pi_{\theta} rather than πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}, and it drives the KL penalty rather than the clipped policy surrogate, so κi,t\kappa_{i,t} must not be identified with ri,tr_{i,t}. This confidence-weighted, KL-regularized GRPO variant (Guo et al., 2025) maximizes

𝒥GRPO​(θ)=𝔼⁡[1G​∑i=1Gwc,d,gconf​1|oi|​∑t(Ji,tclip​(θ)−β​KLi,t​(θ))],\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}w^{\mathrm{conf}}_{c,d,g}\,\frac{1}{|o_{i}|}\sum_{t}\left(J^{\mathrm{clip}}_{i,t}(\theta)-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}_{i,t}(\theta)\right)\right], (40)

so that the per-triplet weight wc,d,gconfw^{\mathrm{conf}}_{c,d,g} multiplies the complete per-response objective—the clipped policy surrogate together with its KL penalty—exactly once, uniformly scaling every parameter update contributed by that triplet without appearing inside A^i\hat{A}_{i} or KLi,t\mathrm{KL}_{i,t}. The token-level clipped surrogate uses the unscaled standardized advantage,

Ji,tclip​(θ)=min⁡(ri,t​(θ)​A^i,clip⁡(ri,t​(θ), 1−ε, 1+ε)​A^i),J^{\mathrm{clip}}_{i,t}(\theta)=\min\!\big(r_{i,t}(\theta)\,\hat{A}_{i},\ \operatorname{clip}(r_{i,t}(\theta),\,1-\varepsilon,\,1+\varepsilon)\,\hat{A}_{i}\big), (41)

and the token-level KL term uses the sampled-token GRPO estimator

KLi,t​(θ)=κi,t​(θ)−log⁡κi,t​(θ)−1,\mathrm{KL}_{i,t}(\theta)=\kappa_{i,t}(\theta)-\log\kappa_{i,t}(\theta)-1, (42)

which is nonnegative for every κi,t​(θ)>0\kappa_{i,t}(\theta)>0 and equals zero exactly when πθ(oi,t∣⋅)=πθSFT(oi,t∣⋅)\pi_{\theta}(o_{i,t}\mid\cdot)=\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{SFT}}}(o_{i,t}\mid\cdot); it estimates the KL divergence from the current policy toward πθSFT\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{SFT}}} using only the sampled token oi,to_{i,t} and never enumerates the full token vocabulary. The clipping term limits the size of policy updates driven by any single batch of rewards, and the KL term toward πθSFT\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{SFT}}}, rather than the continually updated policy, preserves the linguistic competence and reasoning structure established during SFT. We use clipping range ε=0.20\varepsilon=0.20, KL coefficient β=0.01\beta=0.01, and the remaining optimization settings listed in Section 3.

Training monitors.

Throughout training we monitor gene-level accuracy, per-class recall for Up\mathrm{Up}, Down\mathrm{Down}, and No\mathrm{No}, pathway-label accuracy on 𝒫det\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{det}}, output-format pass rate, response length, and policy KL divergence toward πθSFT\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{SFT}}}, so that reward-hacking behaviors such as optimizing format alone, over-predicting majority classes, or gaining indirect advantage through response length rather than correctness can be identified and used to trigger early stopping or hyperparameter adjustment on the training-split validation subset.

A.5 Cross-scale embedding construction

Following GenePT (Chen and Zou, 2025), we treat generated text as an explicit interface between biological knowledge and numerical representation. For each gene gg, PertMind produces a profile pgp_{g} describing its function, interactions, pathways, and context-dependent roles. The raw text embedding and its task-adapted representation are

ug=Eada​(pg)∈ℝ1536,eg(t)=At​ug+bt∈ℝdt,dt∈{512,2048},u_{g}=E_{\mathrm{ada}}(p_{g})\in\mathbb{R}^{1536},\qquad e_{g}^{(t)}=A_{t}u_{g}+b_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{t}},\qquad d_{t}\in\{512,2048\}, (43)

where EadaE_{\mathrm{ada}} denotes text-embedding-ada-002 and At,btA_{t},b_{t} form the learned projection for downstream task tt. The projection permits different decoders to consume a common source representation without claiming that every task shares an identical fixed-dimensional latent space. Whenever a downstream interface requires this adapter, it is reinitialized within each training fold and optimized jointly with the downstream classifier or decoder using only the reference-training partition; query or test labels are never used to fit the projection.

For cell ii, let xi​g≥0x_{ig}\geq 0 be the preprocessed expression of gene gg. We obtain an expression-weighted cell embedding

zi(t)=Normalize⁡(∑g∈𝒢ixi​g​eg(t)∑g∈𝒢ixi​g+ϵ),z_{i}^{(t)}=\operatorname{Normalize}\!\left(\frac{\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}_{i}}x_{ig}e_{g}^{(t)}}{\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}_{i}}x_{ig}+\epsilon}\right), (44)

where 𝒢i\mathcal{G}_{i} is the set of represented genes, ϵ>0\epsilon>0 prevents division by zero, and Normalize\operatorname{Normalize} denotes row-wise unit ℓ2\ell_{2} normalization. For donor dd, the cells ℐd\mathcal{I}_{d} form a multi-instance bag. An attention module computes αd​i=softmaxi∈ℐd⁡(a⁡(zi(t)))\alpha_{di}=\operatorname{softmax}_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{d}}(a(z_{i}^{(t)})) and aggregates

hd(t)=∑i∈ℐdαd​i​zi(t).h_{d}^{(t)}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{d}}\alpha_{di}z_{i}^{(t)}. (45)

The resulting donor embedding is passed to the donor-level classifier. Figure 8 summarizes this gene-to-cell-to-donor hierarchy.

Appendix B Additional Results

This section collects the pre-RL sampling analysis, gene-embedding visualization, per-subject general evaluation, and literature-audited case deferred from the main Results.

Before reinforcement learning, we probed the Base model’s sampling distribution on the forward perturbation task by drawing responses independently for each query up to N=50N=50 rollouts. Here, oracle denotes an evaluation-only rule that uses the gold label to determine whether any sampled response is correct; the model cannot implement this selection at inference time. For a fixed query, best@NN counts the query as correct if any of its first NN sampled responses matches the gold terminal label, whereas majority@NN uses the modal parsed terminal label among those NN responses. We additionally report Δ\Deltabest@NN, the incremental oracle gain contributed by the NN-th rollout, together with the mean parse rate, the any-parse rate, and class-conditional best@NN for No\mathrm{No}, Up\mathrm{Up}, and Down\mathrm{Down}.

Figure 9 shows a sharp early rise in oracle best@NN, followed by diminishing but nonzero gains over later rollouts, which indicates that the pretrained policy already assigns some probability mass to correct answers but does not concentrate it reliably enough for direct use. This quantity is therefore an oracle support diagnostic, not a deployable accuracy estimate and not an inference-time selector. By contrast, majority@NN remains nearly flat around its single-sample level and does not materially improve with additional samples, showing that naive multi-sample voting fails to recover the latent support revealed by best@NN. The format curves rule out parsing as the main bottleneck: the mean parse rate stays close to 1 and the any-parse rate is essentially saturated throughout, so most failures reflect biological decision errors rather than missing terminal labels.

The class-conditional curves further clarify where this support is uneven. Up\mathrm{Up} is recovered most easily and approaches saturation after only a small number of rollouts, Down\mathrm{Down} improves more gradually, and No\mathrm{No} remains the hardest class across the entire range of NN. This separation matters for both DE and DIR: correctly identifying No\mathrm{No} is the main challenge for differential-expression detection, while the persistent gap between Up\mathrm{Up} and Down\mathrm{Down} shows that direction prediction still requires genuine discrimination between the two changed-state labels. Together, these trends motivate policy optimization that increases the concentration of correct outcomes, rather than relying on more sampling or majority voting at inference time.
